subject: chemistry-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

choices: Exothermic, because energy is released when atoms separate
Endothermic, because energy is needed to separate atoms
Endothermic, because energy is released to the surroundings
Exothermic, because the products are more stable than reactants
items.note: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy; forming bonds always releases it. ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).

choices: The enthalpy change depends on the number of steps in the route
Energy is lost as heat at every step of a reaction pathway
The enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken
Enthalpy changes can only be measured directly by calorimetry
items.note: Because enthalpy is a state function, any route from the same reactants to the same products has the same ΔH.

items.stem: The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is:
items.note: By definition ΔHf° = 0 for elements in their standard states (e.g. O₂(g), C(graphite)).

items.stem: Use bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431) to find ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g).
Use bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹: C–H 414, O=O 498, C=O 804, O–H 463) to estimate ΔH for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g).
Using ΔHf° values (kJ mol⁻¹: CH₄ −74, CO₂ −394, H₂O(l) −286), the enthalpy of combustion of methane is:
items.note: ΔHc = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = (−394 + 2(−286)) − (−74) = −892. O₂ has ΔHf = 0.

items.stem: Why is ΔH from average bond enthalpies different from the value found with ΔHf data?
choices: Bond enthalpies are averages from many compounds and apply to gases
Bond enthalpies include the energy of intermolecular forces
ΔHf values are only estimates from calorimetry experiments
Bond enthalpies only apply to reactions at high pressure
items.note: Average bond enthalpies ignore the specific molecular environment, and they assume all species are gaseous.

items.stem: Given: C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g) ΔH = −394 kJ; CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g) ΔH = −283 kJ. Find ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g).
items.note: Route: C → CO₂ (−394), then reverse CO → CO₂ (+283). ΔH = −394 + 283 = −111 kJ.

items.stem: In a Born–Haber cycle for NaCl, which step is exothermic?
items.note: Adding an electron to a Cl atom releases energy (−349 kJ mol⁻¹). Atomisation and ionisation are endothermic.

items.stem: Which equation represents the lattice enthalpy of MgO, as defined in the data booklet?
items.note: The data booklet defines lattice enthalpy as the endothermic separation of the solid into gaseous ions, so values are positive.

items.stem: The second electron affinity of oxygen, O⁻(g) + e⁻ → O²⁻(g), is endothermic because:
choices: Oxygen has a low nuclear charge
The electron enters a new, outer shell
The electron is added to an ion that is already negative
Oxide ions are smaller than oxygen atoms
items.note: Repulsion between O⁻ and the incoming electron must be overcome, so energy is absorbed (about +753 kJ mol⁻¹).

items.stem: Using bond enthalpies (kJ mol⁻¹: C=C 614, C–C 346, C–H 414, H–H 436), calculate ΔH for C₂H₄(g) + H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g).
markscheme: Bonds broken: C=C + 4 C–H + H–H = 614 + 1656 + 436 = 2706 kJ (1)
items.tactic: Draw full structures and count every bond before you add.

items.stem: Explain why the value in the previous question differs from the value found using ΔHf° data (−136 kJ mol⁻¹).
markscheme: Bond enthalpies are average values from a range of compounds (1)
The actual bonds in ethene/ethane differ from the average (1)
items.tactic: Give the reason and say which value is more reliable (ΔHf°).

items.stem: Construct a Born–Haber cycle calculation for the lattice enthalpy of KCl. Data (kJ mol⁻¹): ΔHf(KCl) −437; atomisation K +89; atomisation Cl (½Cl₂ → Cl) +121; first IE of K +419; first EA of Cl −349.
markscheme: ΔHf = ΔHat(K) + ΔHat(Cl) + IE + EA − ΔHlattice (1)
items.tactic: Write the cycle as one equation before substituting; check the sign convention of the data booklet (lattice enthalpy positive).

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) A student measured ΔH for two reactions by calorimetry: (1) MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) ΔH₁ = −146 kJ mol⁻¹; (2) Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) ΔH₂ = −452 kJ mol⁻¹. Given ΔHf(H₂O(l)) = −286 kJ mol⁻¹.
(a) Use Hess's law to determine ΔHf of MgO. (b) The literature value is −602 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the percentage error. (c) Explain why ΔHf of MgO cannot easily be measured directly.
markscheme: (a) Mg + ½O₂ → MgO: ΔH = ΔH₂ − ΔH₁ + ΔHf(H₂O) (1)
(c) Burning Mg gives a very fast, very hot reaction / heat is hard to capture / some Mg may not react completely (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
